intro: A running record of what I'm reading, questioning, and trying to think clearly about. This isn't a set of conclusions — it's a log of an ongoing process. Where something is my own interpretation rather than an established idea, I've tried to say so plainly.
description: I'm not trained in philosophy formally — this section is me thinking in public, not lecturing. Disagreement and correction are welcome.

thinkers.name: J. Krishnamurti
thinkers.description: I'm exploring Krishnamurti's ideas on choiceless awareness and the limits of self-observation. His insistence that the observer is the observed challenges conventional notions of self-improvement through discipline or practice. I'm particularly interested in how this applies to everyday mental habits and the search for clarity without ideological frameworks.

thinkers.name: Albert Camus
thinkers.description: Camus' concept of the absurd — the conflict between our search for meaning and the silent universe — resonates with my own questions about purpose. Rather than offering escape through religion or ideology, he proposes embracing the absurd while continuing to live with passion and integrity. I'm examining what it means to 'keep going' without appeal to external meaning.

thinkers.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
thinkers.description: Through Dostoevsky's novels, I'm exploring questions of free will, moral responsibility, and the psychology of suffering. Works like Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov present characters grappling with ethical choices in psychologically rich ways that philosophical treatises often miss. I'm interested in how fiction can reveal philosophical truths about human nature that abstract reasoning might overlook.

thinkers.name: Ramana Maharshi
thinkers.description: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry practice — repeatedly asking 'Who am I?' to dismantle false identifications — appeals to me as a method of direct investigation rather than a belief system to adopt. Unlike doctrinal teachings, this approach encourages personal experimentation with awareness. I'm exploring how this simple question can undermine habitual assumptions about identity and consciousness.

thinkers.name: Osho
thinkers.description: I find Osho useful primarily as a provocative challenger to conventional thinking, even if many of his specific claims lack credibility. His willingness to question sacred cows — whether religious, political, or psychological — creates intellectual friction that can be valuable for testing one's own assumptions. I engage with him critically, extracting useful challenges while rejecting unfounded doctrines, treating him as a catalyst for inquiry rather than an authority.

notesIntro: Short entries on things I've read, ideas that stayed with me, and questions I haven't resolved yet.
notesDescription: I don't expect every note to become an essay. Sometimes one good question is enough.
